title: Enforce noninstantiability with a private constructor
concept: Utility classes that group static methods and fields (such as java.lang.Math or java.util.Arrays) are not meant to be instantiated. If no constructor is declared, Java provides a default public no-arg constructor, unintentionally making the class instantiable. Attempting to enforce noninstantiability by making the class abstract fails because subclasses can still be instantiated. The proper solution is to provide a single private constructor that throws an AssertionError.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: How do you enforce that a utility class containing only static methods cannot be instantiated?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: Declare a single private constructor that throws an AssertionError. This prevents accidental invocation from within the class and reflection, and blocks subclassing.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: Why is making a utility class `abstract` NOT sufficient to prevent instantiation?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: Because an abstract class can still be subclassed, and the subclass's constructor will implicitly call the super constructor, creating an instance.

quiz.question: What happens if you do not declare any constructor in a utility class?
options: The compiler automatically generates a public, parameterless default constructor
The class becomes noninstantiable by default
The compiler issues a warning
All methods in the class become private

quiz.question: Why should the private constructor of a noninstantiable class throw an AssertionError?
options: To prevent accidental invocation from within the class itself or via reflection
It is required by the Java Language Specification
To enable garbage collection
To allow subclasses to override it

quiz.question: What is a side effect of making all constructors private in a utility class?
options: The class cannot be subclassed, because subclass constructors must invoke a superclass constructor
Static methods can no longer access static fields
The class cannot be imported into other packages
The JVM disables JIT compilation for that class

quiz.question: Which standard Java library class is an example of a noninstantiable utility class?
options: java.util.Collections
java.util.ArrayList
java.lang.Thread
java.io.File

quiz.question: Why does making a utility class `abstract` mislead API consumers?
options: It implies the class was designed for inheritance and encourages subclassing
It prevents static methods from being called
It causes compilation errors in Java 17+
It makes the class incompatible with interfaces

interview_questions.question: Why is declaring a private constructor the only foolproof way to enforce noninstantiability?
interview_questions.model_answer: Omitting a constructor causes the compiler to insert a default public constructor. Marking the class abstract misleadingly suggests inheritance and allows subclasses to be instantiated. A private constructor blocks external callers and subclassing, and throwing an `AssertionError` inside defends against internal or reflective invocation.

interview_questions.question: A developer writes `public abstract class MathUtils { ... }` with all static helper methods. What is the design issue?
interview_questions.model_answer: Clients can subclass `MathUtils` and instantiate the subclass, defeating noninstantiability. Furthermore, the `abstract` keyword falsely signals to developers that the class was designed for extension.

interview_questions.question: Does a private constructor completely prevent instantiation via reflection?
interview_questions.model_answer: No, reflection with `setAccessible(true)` can invoke private constructors. That is specifically why Joshua Bloch recommends throwing an exception (like `AssertionError`) inside the constructor body, so reflective calls fail at runtime.

interview_questions.question: How do modern languages like Kotlin or C# handle noninstantiable utility classes compared to Java?
interview_questions.model_answer: Kotlin provides top-level functions and `object` declarations, eliminating utility classes. C# provides the `static class` keyword, where the compiler enforces that no constructors or instance members can exist.
